title: Build Automation
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of build automation and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to build automation.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on build automation. Build automation installs locked dependencies and produces validated outputs that can be retained as artifacts and promoted without rebuilding. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Build Automation matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Build automation installs locked dependencies and produces validated outputs that can be retained as artifacts and promoted without rebuilding. A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Producing build artifacts
items.text: Use an artifact for a file produced by a run, choose exact upload/download paths, set retention intentionally, and verify the downloaded file is from the intended run/job.

items.title: Validating build outputs
items.text: Use an artifact for a file produced by a run, choose exact upload/download paths, set retention intentionally, and verify the downloaded file is from the intended run/job.

items.title: Separating build and test stages
items.text: Use filters to reduce unnecessary runs only when skipped work is genuinely unrelated. Include shared dependencies and test the changed and unchanged path cases so required checks are not bypassed.

items.title: Reproducible build practices
items.text: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. Preserve reports where useful and configure required branch checks to match the checks the workflow actually emits.

content_blocks.code:
name: Test and report
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Run project tests here"

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain build automation, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Build CI checks that produce repeatable evidence and protect merge quality.

content.task: Apply build automation to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Build automation installs locked dependencies and produces validated outputs that can be retained as artifacts and promoted without rebuilding.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Build automation installs locked dependencies and produces validated outputs that can be retained as artifacts and promoted without rebuilding. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
